690: Or whether he is sitting - However, he makes the blessing while standing.

But he should not read - This means to say that if one is reading for the congregation, he needs to read standing. See the Be'er Hetev where we bring an opinion that standing through leaning is permitted regarding the Megillah reading.

And it is forbidden for the Chazzan - Because leading the congregation is an honor, and it is inappropriate for a person to assign himself honor before they honor him. This applies when it is not a fixed position, but a fixed shaliach tzibbur (the one who leads the services) who was appointed for this, they do not need to wait.

And they fulfil their obligation - And we don't say that 'two voices cannot be heard properly' as is in the case of reading the Torah and other cases, since this reading is especially beloved due to the miracle, and people focus their attention to hear it well. Since this is so, if someone feels that these many voices are confusing him, and that it is impossible for him to hear all the words, he certainly has not fulfilled his obligation.
He needs to read the entire thing - And this is an invalidating factor. It is the opinion of most authorities that even if one missed a single word, he has not fulfilled his obligation.

And [he must read it] from inside the scroll itself - The Talmud explains that even if one reads every single verse properly, except that it was from a non-Kosher scroll, that act is considered as if he recited it by-heart, and he has not fulfilled his obligation.

And he needs to have the full scroll [in front of him] - Meaning: all that we said about not fulfilling one's obligation only applies if he recited a majority of the Megillah by heart. But if he only recited part of it, it is valid post facto. This applies even if the reason for the by-heart recital was because the scribe omitted as much as half of the words in the middle, and the reader was forced to read the rest orally. Even-though ideally, it is incorrect to use an incomplete Megillah, nevertheless, one fulfils their obligation after-the-fact.
But after-the-fact - If there is no alternative Megillah, one should use it (the scroll with missing words) from the beginning.
Even up to half - Once you get to half [of the words missing], we must consider if after-the-fact, it is valid.

But if he omitted - In this case, it appears like a missing book. This is unlike when a verse is omitted in the middle, since it is just a complete book with mistakes, and one does not need to be meticulous with the Megillah in this regard. This is as long as the errors are not the majority of the Megillah, since it is considered a letter.
Even if it is only a little [of the beginning] - And it is possible that even if only the first or last verse is missing, the ruling is the same.
Specifically, where a complete section was not omitted - because if a complete section is omitted, it appears like an incomplete book.

He shouldn't read [aloud] - For perhaps the listener will pay attention to the one reading and not to the reader. Based on this, if one is reading for just one person, he is permitted to read from a non-Kosher Megillah or from a Chumash. However, there are those who are stringent in all cases, since the listener is focusing on his reading and not paying attention to what the reader says, since he is engrossed in the reading itself.

He also shouldn't assist - This is for the same reason as above, see the Eliya-Rabbah who supports being stringent here — even when reading for one person — because perhaps the listener will pay attention to what he himself is reading aloud, and in the meantime, a few words that the reader reads may be omitted.

And therefore, those verses [which the congregation reads] - That is to say, similar to the case where they are stringent not to assist out loud, since it causes people to focus on the one assisting, whereas in reality, it should ideally be read entirely from the scroll itself. Likewise, in this case (the verses that the congregation say together), the reader must go back and read from a kosher Megillah, while the listeners have in mind to fulfil their obligation with his reading, so that it is all from the scroll.
The reader needs - This is only in an ideal situation.
